summary.text: The rule of product, or multiplication principle, is a basic counting principle in combinatorics.
If there are a ways of doing one thing and b ways of doing another, there are a · b ways of doing both.
When you pick one of two crusts and then one of three toppings, the rule gives 2 × 3 = 6 possible pizzas.

facts.label: The formula
facts.value: a ways and b ways give a · b ways for both

facts.label: Infinite sets
facts.value: The sets need not be finite

facts.label: Companion rule
facts.value: The rule of sum covers things you cannot do together

items.prompt: A shop sells 4 kinds of shirt and 3 kinds of trousers. You pick one of each. How many different outfits can you make?

options.label: 7 outfits
12 outfits
1 outfit
24 outfits

items.explain: You do both actions, a ways and b ways, so the count is a · b: 4 × 3 = 12.

items.prompt: You must pick one of 2 crusts and then one of 3 toppings. Why does the number of pizzas come from multiplying and not from adding?

options.label: Because multiplying always gives the bigger answer
Because the toppings are chosen before the crusts
Because crusts and toppings cannot be mixed together
Because every crust can be paired with each topping

items.explain: Both choices are made, and each of the 2 crusts goes with each of the 3 toppings, giving 2 × 3 = 6 pizzas.

items.prompt: For lunch you will pick one meal from 3 soups or one meal from 4 salads, never both. Which counting idea gives the number of lunch choices?

options.label: Add them, because the two options cannot be done at once
Multiply them, because there are two kinds of option
Subtract them, because you give up one kind
Neither, because the choices have different sizes

items.explain: When two things cannot be done at the same time, the ways to choose one of them are added. That is the rule of sum, not the rule of product.

items.prompt: A student claims the multiplication principle only works when every set involved has a limited number of members. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, infinite sets cannot be multiplied at all
Yes, but only when there are exactly two sets
No, the sets need not be finite
No, but it fails if the sets have equal size

items.explain: The sets need not be finite, and there need not be only finitely many factors in the product.

items.prompt: A pizza place has 2 crusts and 3 toppings. It then offers twice as many crusts and keeps the same toppings. What happens to the number of combinations?

options.label: It rises by 2
It stays the same
It rises by 3
It doubles

items.explain: The total is a · b, so doubling the crust choices while keeping b fixed doubles the product.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly separates the rule of product from the rule of sum?

options.label: Product counts doing both actions; sum counts choosing one of two actions that cannot happen together
Product counts choosing one of two actions; sum counts doing both actions together
Product is for big numbers; sum is for small numbers of choices
Product is for finite sets; sum is for infinite sets of choices

items.explain: The rule of product applies when you perform both actions, giving a · b. The rule of sum applies when the actions cannot both be done, giving a + b.
